name: Preoptic area
function: Rostral hypothalamic/preoptic region containing multiple medial and lateral cell groups. It participates in heat dissipation, reproductive neuroendocrine control and sleep promotion; GABAergic/galaninergic ventrolateral preoptic neurons inhibit arousal systems. This whole-area record combines paired and midline components rather than one discrete midline nucleus.

afferent: Retina indirectly via the suprachiasmatic nucleus (day-length signal)
Brainstem noradrenergic (locus coeruleus) and serotonergic arousal systems
Limbic input from the septal nuclei and amygdala
efferent: Median eminence GnRH neurons to the hypophyseal portal system
Descending thermoregulatory projections to brainstem and spinal autonomic nuclei
Inhibitory (GABAergic/galaninergic) projections to the tuberomammillary nucleus and locus coeruleus (sleep induction)

bloodSupply: Anterior communicating and anterior cerebral artery perforators (rostral hypothalamus), with proximal posterior communicating contributions.

clinical.findings: Anterior hypothalamic/preoptic injury can cause hyperthermia or insomnia, with severity depending on the affected circuits. Fatal familial insomnia is predominantly a thalamic prion disorder and should not be used as a specific preoptic lesion example.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and hormone deficiency, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Suprachiasmatic nucleus
function: Paired circadian timing nuclei immediately above the optic chiasm. Specialized melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells provide retinohypothalamic input that entrains daily rhythms; SCN output coordinates hypothalamic and autonomic pathways influencing sleep timing and pineal melatonin.

afferent: Melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells through the retinohypothalamic tract
Additional modulatory retinal/thalamic/brainstem inputs
efferent: Hypothalamic circadian networks
Multisynaptic autonomic pathway through paraventricular region, spinal sympathetic neurons and superior cervical ganglion to pineal gland

bloodSupply: Anterior communicating artery perforators and proximal posterior communicating/PCA branches (rostral hypothalamic perforators).

clinical.findings: SCN-region injury can disrupt daily timing of sleep and endocrine rhythms. Blindness may reduce photic entrainment when nonvisual retinal input is lost; shift work causes circadian misalignment without implying anatomical SCN damage.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and hormone deficiency, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Supraoptic nucleus
function: Magnocellular neurosecretory nucleus manufacturing vasopressin (ADH) — with some oxytocin neurons: axons run through the infundibulum to the posterior pituitary, where ADH released into blood acts on renal V2 receptors to conserve water; lamina-terminalis osmoreceptors and baroreceptor pathways set its firing rate.

afferent: Organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis and subfornical organ (osmolality and angiotensin II signals)
Nucleus solitarius baroreceptor afferents (volume status)
efferent: Posterior pituitary via the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract of the infundibulum (vasopressin and oxytocin release)

bloodSupply: Superior hypophyseal and anterior communicating/ACA perforators (rostral hypothalamic group).

clinical.findings: Sufficient injury to the hypothalamic-neurohypophyseal system can cause central diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency), with dilute polyuria and thirst. Hypernatremia develops particularly when water intake cannot match losses, rather than occurring in every patient.
SIADH has many neurologic and nonneurologic causes and is not a diagnosis of isolated supraoptic nuclear damage.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and hormone deficiency, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Paraventricular nucleus (hypothalamus)
function: The hypothalamic autonomic-neuroendocrine integrator: magnocellular neurons release oxytocin and vasopressin from the posterior pituitary, parvocellular CRH and TRH neurons drive the HPA and thyroid axes, and descending projections to the intermediolateral column and dorsal vagal complex orchestrate sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow.

afferent: Subfornical organ and organum vasculosum (angiotensin II, osmotic signals)
Nucleus solitarius visceral (baroreceptor, chemoreceptor) afferents
Suprachiasmatic nucleus (circadian timing) and limbic input
efferent: Posterior pituitary via the infundibulum (oxytocin, vasopressin)
Median eminence portal system (CRH to ACTH; TRH to TSH)
Intermediolateral cell column (T1-L2) and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (autonomic outflow)

bloodSupply: Superior hypophyseal/anterior communicating perforators rostrally and paramedian posterior communicating/PCA branches.

clinical.findings: PVN-region injury may affect vasopressin/oxytocin production, hypothalamic releasing hormones and autonomic control. Broader hypothalamic/stalk lesions can cause central endocrine deficits; paroxysmal sympathetic hyperactivity is a distributed brain-injury syndrome and does not uniquely localize to PVN.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and hormone deficiency, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Arcuate nucleus (hypothalamus)
function: Tuberal hypothalamic nucleus adjacent to the median eminence. Multiple neuronal populations contribute to energy balance and hypothalamic endocrine regulation, including dopamine inhibition of prolactin and growth-hormone/reproductive regulation. Hunger- and satiety-related populations coexist, so an orexigenic center is not a synonym for the entire nucleus.

afferent: Leptin and insulin signals (humoral, via the semi-permeable median eminence)
Ghrelin from the stomach (direct and vagal)
Lateral hypothalamic orexin/MCH neurons
efferent: Paraventricular and dorsomedial nuclei (melanocortin and NPY projections)
Median eminence: GHRH and tuberoinfundibular dopamine (prolactin-inhibiting factor) to the portal system
KNDy (kisspeptin/neurokinin B/dynorphin) projections to the GnRH neurons — the pulse generator of the reproductive axis

bloodSupply: Superior hypophyseal artery (median eminence portal capillary bed) and paramedian hypothalamic perforators of the posterior communicating/PCA.

clinical.findings: Medial hypothalamic injury can contribute to obesity through altered appetite, energy expenditure and endocrine/autonomic mechanisms. The human syndrome cannot be assigned solely to a single arcuate or ventromedial nucleus.
Interruption of hypothalamic dopamine delivery to the anterior pituitary can raise prolactin. The effect reflects the delivery pathway and is not proof of selective arcuate nuclear loss.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and hormone deficiency, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Ventromedial nucleus (hypothalamus)
function: Medial tuberal hypothalamic nucleus involved in energy balance, glucose regulation and behavioral/autonomic responses. Classical lesion/stimulation studies, mainly in animals, link it to feeding and defensive behavior; human hypothalamic obesity and aggression are distributed circuit phenomena.

afferent: Arcuate nucleus melanocortin/NPY projections (leptin-ghrelin signal)
Amygdala and hippocampus via the ventral amygdalofugal pathway
Lateral hypothalamic area
efferent: Lateral hypothalamic area and paraventricular nucleus (autonomic/endocrine coordination)
Periaqueductal gray (defensive behavior)
Brainstem and spinal autonomic centers (glucoregulation)

bloodSupply: Paramedian hypothalamic perforators (posterior communicating and P1/PCA branches); anterior choroidal contributions laterally.

clinical.findings: Lesions of medial hypothalamic networks may cause obesity, endocrine and autonomic changes. Experimental VMH lesion/stimulation findings do not establish a fixed human syndrome of voracious appetite, rage or autonomic storms from selective VMH injury.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and hormone deficiency, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Dorsomedial nucleus (hypothalamus)
function: Rhythm and stress-coordination nucleus linking the suprachiasmatic clock to feeding and sleep-wake cycles: DMH neurons generate anticipatory locomotor and feeding rhythms and recruit endocrine (paraventricular) and autonomic outputs during stress.

afferent: Suprachiasmatic nucleus (daily timing signal)
Lateral hypothalamic orexin neurons
Paraventricular and arcuate nuclei
efferent: Paraventricular nucleus (HPA axis recruitment)
Preoptic sleep-wake systems and locus coeruleus
Brainstem autonomic nuclei

bloodSupply: Paramedian hypothalamic perforators (posterior communicating and P1) and posterior choroidal territory borders.

clinical.findings: DMH participates in hypothalamic timing and autonomic networks. Precise effects of selective human DMH lesions are poorly established; night-eating, hypersomnia or autonomic storms should not be used as unique nuclear-localization rules.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and hormone deficiency, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Posterior hypothalamic nucleus
function: Posterior hypothalamic region participating in heat conservation and arousal. Nearby tuberomammillary histamine and lateral hypothalamic orexin systems contribute to wakefulness but are anatomically distinct populations rather than synonyms for the posterior hypothalamic nucleus.

afferent: Preoptic/anterior hypothalamic warm-signal projections (thermoregulatory loop)
Limbic and reticular arousal inputs
efferent: Dorsal vagal complex and intermediolateral column (pressor and heat-conservation sympathetic drive)
Tuberomammillary histaminergic system, then widespread cortical arousal
Descending reticular formation projections

bloodSupply: Paramedian hypothalamic perforators of the P1/PCA and posterior communicating artery; anterior choroidal branches laterally.

clinical.findings: Bilateral posterior hypothalamic injury may impair thermoregulation and cause hypersomnia. Kleine-Levin syndrome and episodic hypothermia have uncertain/distributed mechanisms; they do not prove selective posterior-nuclear failure.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and hormone deficiency, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Mammillary body
function: Paired ventral posterior hypothalamic mammillary bodies participate in episodic/spatial memory networks. They receive postcommissural fornical input and project to anterior thalamus through the mammillothalamic tract, with tegmental connections as well. They are vulnerable in thiamine-deficiency disease, but are not a universally proven first site of failure.

afferent: Hippocampal formation via the fornix (postcommissural fibers to the medial mammillary nuclei)
Gudden tegmental nuclei (mammillotegmental feedback loop)
efferent: Anterior thalamic nucleus via the mammillothalamic tract (tract of Vicq d'Azyr)
Midbrain tegmentum via the mammillotegmental tract

bloodSupply: Paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) branches of the P1/PCA and posterior communicating artery perforators.

clinical.findings: Wernicke/Korsakoff disease can involve mammillary, medial thalamic and additional periventricular/frontal networks. The classic acute triad, later confabulation or mammillary atrophy is not obligatory. Injury to mammillothalamic/anterior thalamic pathways can also impair memory without thiamine deficiency.

name: Hypothalamus (context envelope)
function: Silhouette of the hypothalamic wedge — the floor and lateral walls of the third ventricle from the optic chiasm to the mammillary bodies, bounding the tuber cinereum — used on the sagittal plate and in the 3D scene; the individual nuclei are separate records.
contextNote: Envelope/block tag for the hypothalamic wedge silhouette on the sagittal plate and in the 3D scene; not a nucleus record (see the individual hypothalamic nucleus records).

afferent: Limbic, viscerosensory and reticular inputs converging on the hypothalamus (see individual nuclei)
efferent: Pituitary (portal system and posterior lobe) and brainstem/spinal autonomic nuclei

bloodSupply: Circle-of-Willis perforators: anterior communicating and superior hypophyseal rostrally, posterior communicating paramedially, P1/PCA branches caudally.

clinical.findings: Lesions may affect vision, growth, water balance, appetite, temperature and endocrine function according to the involved structures. Pediatric diencephalic wasting is a particular tumor-associated presentation, not the universal hypothalamic syndrome.
Hypothalamic/pituitary-stalk injury can cause DI, transient inappropriate antidiuresis or, occasionally, a triphasic response. Persistent dysfunction depends on injury extent.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic nuclei and regional functions, printed pp. 792-797 (PDF pp. 818-823).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, water balance and hormone deficiency, printed pp. 803-804 (PDF pp. 829-830).

name: Optic chiasm
function: Optic pathway crossing on the ventral anterior diencephalon near the suprasellar region. Nasal retinal fibers cross while temporal retinal fibers remain ipsilateral. It lies beneath the anterior hypothalamus and anterior/superior to the pituitary stalk; central compression can produce bitemporal visual field loss.

afferent: Retinal ganglion cell axons from both optic nerves
efferent: Optic tracts to the lateral geniculate nuclei, pretectum and superior colliculi
Retinohypothalamic fibers to the suprachiasmatic nuclei

bloodSupply: Superior hypophyseal and anterior communicating branches superiorly; internal carotid and posterior communicating branches inferiorly (segmental supply underlies chiasmal infarction).

clinical.findings: Compression by pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma or meningioma strikes the decussating nasal fibers — progressive loss of both temporal visual fields, often with endocrine signs.
clinical.note: mass effect at the sellar/suprasellar junction

clinical.findings: Rare chiasmal infarction (or apoplectic pituitary tumor) presents with acute bitemporal field loss and headache.
clinical.vascular: Superior hypophyseal and anterior communicating perforators

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 11, optic chiasm and tracts, printed pp. 463-464 (PDF pp. 489-490).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 11, visual fields and blood supply, printed pp. 472-477 (PDF pp. 498-503).
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed. (2010), Ch. 17, hypothalamic relationships, printed pp. 792-795 (PDF pp. 818-821).

name: Infundibulum (pituitary stalk)
function: The pituitary stalk carrying the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal vessels and magnocellular axons from the tuber cinereum to the pituitary; transection or compression interrupts dopamine, CRH/TRH delivery and ADH axons — the basis of the 'stalk effect' and traumatic diabetes insipidus.

afferent: Tuberoinfundibular dopamine fibers from the arcuate nucleus
Magnocellular supraoptic and paraventricular axons
Median eminence portal capillaries
efferent: Anterior pituitary (portal blood carrying releasing and inhibiting hormones)
Posterior pituitary (ADH and oxytocin nerve terminals)

bloodSupply: Superior hypophyseal branches, usually from internal carotid/posterior communicating region, supply median eminence and portal-system structures; inferior hypophyseal branches supply the posterior pituitary.

clinical.findings: Compression or injury can interrupt dopamine delivery (hyperprolactinemia), hypothalamic-releasing hormone delivery, or vasopressin axons. DI and anterior-pituitary deficits depend on injury site and extent.
After pituitary-region surgery or trauma, some patients develop initial DI, transient antidiuresis, then recurrent DI. The sequence and permanent DI are not inevitable.
